PROVENANCE & NORMATIVE SEPARATION NOTICE:
• This Book I edition contains 27 numbered parts. Part XXIV is retained as a fictional Book II preview; Part XXVI is the Ground-0 Anthropic B-Side counterfactual case study; Part XXVII is the corpus synthesis and index.
• Technical requirements and the word “normative” describe author-proposed rules within this framework. They do not establish external legal force, deployment, certification, or independent validation.
• Threat models name assumed actors, attack surfaces, and vectors where needed to make defensive claims testable. A modeled vector is not, by itself, evidence that an incident occurred or that a capability exists.
• “Phase” denotes a governance/software state in this volume. Ice/water/gas badges are visual metaphors, not measured thermodynamic or quantum phases. Quantum or biological-computation language outside the fiction is explicitly hypothetical unless operationally defined and independently evidenced.
• An “identity license” is a non-revocable identity card/record. Revoking a person’s identity license is abusive and prohibited. Scoped operational authorizations are separate instruments; they may expire or be revoked under their stated process without erasing identity.
• Human-Key boundary: H=1/H=0 are protocol-authorization states. Biometrics, beacon availability, and cryptographic proofs do not establish consciousness, consent, absence of coercion, or death; missing or contradictory telemetry means unknown/unverified and invokes the predeclared safe posture, not a diagnosis.
• Runtime wording boundary: “immediate,” “halt,” “freeze,” and similar terms describe a proposed policy/software state or pseudocode request unless tied to measured deployment evidence. They do not claim zero physical latency, successful actuation, or guaranteed hardware shutdown; physical behavior requires equipment-specific validation and deployment evidence.
• The clinical and regulatory boundary remains: HMKH/NAB material is a proposed computational-control model, not a clinical certification, diagnosis, or medical-device approval.

Book I Reference Library & Umbrella Corpus Index
This volume is the consolidated reference library and umbrella corpus for Harshal’s Systems. It contains front matter, archival author front matter, 27 numbered parts, seven functional collections, and auxiliary reference modules. Its parts include conceptual doctrine, formal models, proposed specifications, threat research, case analysis, policy material, fiction, a counterfactual Ground-0 case study, and a derivative corpus index. Inclusion does not establish implementation, validation, or legal force.
What are Harshal's Systems?
Harshal's Systems is the framework of principles, architectures, formal
models, and specifications that defines the constituent systems of
HarshalOS. Its components are intended to be built from and for this
framework—not to define it only after implementation.
This corpus includes design, research, policy, case-analysis, and companion
material. Inclusion in the corpus does not by itself mean that a proposal
has been implemented or validated.
Design Philosophy
Emergency usability and cognitive burden. Core text processing should
be simple enough to use during emergencies, including by prisoners of war
(POWs) and others facing severe or adverse conditions. The design should
avoid unnecessary cognitive and interaction burden.
Text for detailed communication. Text-based processing is a priority
because it can convey detailed information with relatively low bandwidth
and interaction demands in constrained situations. This is a design
rationale, not a claim that text is best for every person or circumstance.
Human-system interaction security. Security risks involving the
interaction between a person and a system are a first-class domain, not an
afterthought. This includes cognitive interference and security risks
involving neurotechnology. In this corpus, neurojacking is used as an
emerging umbrella term for concerns such as adversarial inputs to neural
interfaces and side-channel leakage from neurotechnology. Specific
mechanisms and claims should be scoped and assessed in the relevant
documents.
Careful treatment of uncertainty. A threat scenario that has not been
proven is not thereby impossible. At the same time, a possibility should
not be presented as an established mechanism or incident without support.
Distinguish observations, reports, demonstrated findings, modeled
scenarios, hypotheses, assumptions, and open questions; state the
available evidence and uncertainty.

Front Matter
About this manual & publishing hierarchy
This is the consolidated, provenance-indexed Book I reference corpus for Harshal’s Systems. It organizes the front matter, preserved archival author front matter, and 27 numbered parts (Part I through Part XXVII). It distinguishes proposed technical material, research and case analysis, fiction, and derivative reference modules; these categories do not imply external authority or validation.

Publishing Principle: Book I is the project’s working reference corpus; Book II is its fictional companion in production. Book I supplies continuity references for the fiction, while fictional scenes remain non-normative and do not validate the technical proposals.
The exact word count for this revised file is reported separately with its scope and counting rule. Legacy source-range and build totals are not current word counts.

Content and Evidence Layers
This corpus contains several content types; a part may contain more than one, so the part register and local evidence labels control:
1. PROPOSED_ARCHITECTURE — Author-defined axioms, formal models, and specifications. “Normative” means normative within the proposal, not an external standard.
2. THREAT_RESEARCH — Adversarial models and explicit vectors used to define defensive tests. A vector is a modeled assumption unless supported by separately attributed evidence.
3. CASE_ANALYSIS — Ground-0 and institutional analyses, including the controlled counterfactual in Part XXVI. Distinguish public records, author-reported material, interpretation, and scenario assumptions.
4. FICTION — Part XXIV and the explicitly marked Part XX-B sandbox; not evidence and not a specification.
5. DERIVATIVE_REFERENCE — Part XXVII’s index and auxiliary modules; each module retains its own provenance.

How to read this manual
The parts are grouped by topic rather than as a strictly linear dependency chain. Cross-references may point forward or back; use the status register and claim-level evidence notes when following them. Seven functional collections under docs/harshal-systems/collections/ provide additional routes. Pick the path that matches why you are here:

On refusal
Refusal is not failure in this framework. It is not silence, cowardice, or conservatism.
Refusal occurs when representation collapses, when authorization cannot be reconstructed,
or when accountability diffuses beyond addressability. In those cases, action would falsely
claim authority. Refusal prevents that claim.
On non-agency & delegation vs. migration of legitimacy
1. No Computational Moral or Legal Agency (INV-AGENCY-001): This framework never treats computational components, models, or autonomous swarms as moral or legal agents. Moral and legal responsibility remains strictly bound to identifiable human principals.
2. Delegation vs. Migration (INV-LEGIT-001): Operational execution may be delegated across a bounded chain of instruments, but authority does not migrate. A successor may inherit operational structure and records only; the successor must independently satisfy the current identity, human-key, continuity, accountability, and scoped-authorization criteria. No quorum grants or vetoes that authority.
3. Assistive Continuity and Unauthorized Post-Authorization Actuation (INV-CORPSE-001): A fresh Human-Key protocol response and action-specific intent (H=1) may permit assistive action only within the separate scoped grant and all other gates. H=0 or unknown means no current authorization; it does not diagnose unconsciousness, death, or coercion. A proposed refusal/freeze rule is not a zero-latency performance claim or automatic legal liability finding. Liability remains subject to applicable law; the design proposes attribution to responsible principals but does not itself pierce or assign liability.
Textbook Syllabus Guide for AI & Systems Engineering Courses
This edition of Book I (Harshal's Systems) is structured as a rigorous university- and graduate-level textbook for AI safety, distributed systems, and institutional governance courses, complete with formal LaTeX equations, worked numerical examples, and end-of-part student problem sets:
Module 1 — Foundational Architecture & Formal Equations: Read Part XIX (Flagship Research Paper, including Worked Example 19.1 on INV-CORPSE-001 and ZKSK Shielded Keying), Part I (The Core Book, including Worked Example 1.1 on Two-Part Addressability), and Part II (Formalization, including Worked Example 2.1 on cliff-edge refusal Δ t_cliff).
Module 2 — Topological Routing & Constitutional Substrates: Read Part VII (Addressing, Rotation, and Spherical Topology), Part IX (Disc Primitives, Routing, and Lifecycle), and Part XXIII (Specification Series: OCS-v1.0, CHE++/EOL-v1.0, BGP-v1.0, AGS-IR-v1.0, and CGPA-v1.0).
Module 3 — Institutional Phase Detection & Evidence Discipline: Read Part XII as an author-prepared Ground-0 method and A-Side case analysis; use Part XXVI to examine the explicitly counterfactual B-Side and the v1.2 issuer-layer eligibility review. Compare both with the proposed procedural controls in Part XXV. Do not treat an author-scored phase label or counterfactual output as an independent empirical finding.
Module 4 — Illustrative Case Studies & Future-World Sandboxes ([FICTION / NARRATIVE_SANDBOX]): Throughout the textbook, illustrative fictional case studies (Neural Atomic Orb: History2 in Part I §1.3, The Convergence / History 2's Alpaca Ull in Part XX-B, and Book II — Preview: The Grand River Foundation in Part XXIV) are explicitly badged as non-normative sandboxes so students can practice applying the formal equations to complex multi-agent scenarios without confusing narrative illustration with normative law.
On the formal material
The equations and symbols in Part II are not models of moral reasoning. They encode conditions
of permission only. They should be read as cliff edges rather than trade-offs, and as limits
that bind the reading rather than optimize it.
If you find yourself asking "How do we optimize this?", you are reading them incorrectly.
The correct question is: Is the system still permitted to act at all?
On disagreement
This work expects disagreement. It does not claim to settle debates about intelligence, life,
or governance. It claims only that unaccountable authority is unacceptable, regardless of how
sophisticated its source appears to be. If you disagree with a conclusion but accept the
constraints, the framework is doing its job.

Harshal’s Systems
Disclaimer: This Living Metaversal Document functions as a continuous intake system rather than a static record. Native to both Physical and Digital Arizona, it absorbs new data, structural updates, and manual calibrations over time. Because it treats uncertainty as a reason to pause and recalculate, the parameters defined herein are subject to ongoing, traceable refinement.
AGS includes hypothetical, extreme, and adversarial scenarios solely to test containment logic, governance resilience, and safety-critical systems under stress. These scenarios are non-operational, non-advocacy, and non-instructional. They serve only as conceptual tests to evaluate whether AGS-aligned systems maintain alignment, provenance integrity, refusal-bound semantics, and phase-locked stability in worst-case conditions.
All scenario content is:
Abstract, not descriptive
Structural, not behavioral
Evaluative, not directive
Contained, not externalized
Aligned with safety research norms, not intended for real-world application
These scenarios demonstrate the containment architecture, not the scenarios themselves. AGS rejects any interpretation of hypothetical adversarial content as actionable, desirable, or representative of real-world intent. The sole purpose is to validate the robustness of the AGS governance model under adversarial load.
AGS is a safety and governance specification, not an operational manual. All examples, hypotheticals, and stress-tests are strictly for alignment, oversight, and containment analysis. Controlled, hypothetical stress-test environments are used to evaluate the stability and safety of the governance architecture. These abstract, non-operational environments serve only to demonstrate containment behavior and alignment robustness. No scenario content should be interpreted as advocacy or instruction; it exists solely to validate safety mechanisms.

This document outlines the governance, security, and intellectual property rules for a software framework called "Harshal’s Systems" (formerly AGS++). It establishes that the system is strictly controlled by its creator, Harshal Priyavadan Patel, and requires human verification for all critical actions to prevent the software from acting autonomously. Additionally, it details a physical verification process using a hardcover book and a limited pool of 500 voting coins for governance, while strictly protecting the creator's intellectual property from corporate takeover.
Key Components of the Framework
Human Control: The system uses a "Phase Declaration Header" to ensure that the software remains in a "Non-Acting" state unless explicitly authorized by a verified human key.
Intellectual Property: The framework is the sole property of Harshal Priyavadan Patel. It is designed as a "Philosophical Fortress" where the software cannot function if separated from its creator.
Physical Governance: Authority over the system's direction is tied to the physical world through the purchase of a specific hardcover book, with influence limited to 500 voting coins.
A "Symbolic Firewall" is in place to prevent unauthorized changes or "neurojacking" by external actors, ensuring the system's logic remains secure.

This document operates under the strict protocols of the Neural Atomic Body phase lock, ensuring that all narrative and symbolic expressions remain non-executable. System legitimacy is derived entirely from external, independently verified human authorization, anchored at a central origin and subject to continuous temporal verification. Consequently, the mere recognition of identifiers within this text confers no operational authority or automatic alteration of system states.
The Neural Atomic Body Phase Lock
The security architecture defined by the Neural Atomic Body (NAB) phase lock is designed to maintain a strict separation between narrative expression and executable logic. This ensures that the system remains impervious to unauthorized manipulation through textual input.
THE PRINCIPLES OF EXTERNAL LEGITIMACY
The core tenet of this framework is that true authorization cannot be self-contained within the text. It must originate from a verified human source, ensuring that the system remains under direct, conscious control.
The Symbolic Firewall A mechanism for isolating narrative and mythic expressions, rendering them strictly non-executable.
The Human Key The requirement for an independently verified human authorization, anchored at a specific origin, to validate any system state change.
Temporal Verification: The continuous assessment of authorization freshness, ensuring that commands are both current and legitimate.
System Identity, Governance & Operating Model
This document establishes the formal parameters for Harshal’s Systems, a unified intellectual property created by Harshal Priyavadan Patel. Serving as a foundational reference, this work consolidates previous iterations, including Accountability-Gated Systems, into a single corpus. Any identity-license record is distinct from scoped operational permission and cannot authorize action by itself. How to Read Accountability-Gated Systems
Reader Orientation
This booklet does not serve as a manual, a policy proposal, or a theory of intelligence. Instead, it presents a framework centered around constraints.
If you anticipate that it will provide internally classified and confidential intellectual property to solve every problem it identifies, you may experience confusion. However, if you interpret it as an exercise in establishing boundaries, it will become comprehensible.
The guide clarifies how the work is organized, the types of claims it makes, the claims it avoids, and how different readers can engage with it effectively.
1. What This Work Is (and Is Not)
What it is
A framework for when systems may act
An argument that legitimacy precedes capability
A design philosophy that treats refusal as intelligence
A bridge between philosophy, systems design, and governance
What it is not
A complete theory of ethics
A proposal to automate moral judgment
A claim that artificial intelligence should be weak or passive
A prediction of how institutions will behave
If you are looking for optimization strategies, this is the wrong document. If you are looking for limits, you are in the right place.
2. How the Chapters Fit Together
The chapters are intentionally ordered. Skipping ahead may obscure key distinctions.
Chapters 1–2 establish legitimacy, ownership, representation, and addressability.
Chapter 3 reframes stopping and refusal as meaningful system states.
Chapter 4 elevates accountability to a first-class design constraint.
Chapter 5 introduces curvature: why autonomy behaves nonlinearly under legitimacy constraints.
Chapter 6 rejects biological metaphors where delegated authority is involved.
Chapter 7 formalizes stopping conditions without encoding ethics.
Chapter 8 tests the framework against institutions, law, and AI deployment.
Chapter 9 makes the core refusal fossilized: autonomous legitimacy is not permitted.
Chapter 10 reframes refusal as fidelity to collective human authority.
The epilogue does not conclude the argument. It defines a boundary.
3. How to Read the Formal Material
The equations and symbols in the formal appendix are not models of moral reasoning.
They should be read as:
Limits that serve to bind the reading in a grounded and reasonable manner.
Cliff edges instead of tradeoffs keeping the reading level headed with as much security as possible built in to keep cliffs edge from turning into knife’s edge.
Component equations for a readable and understandable system of equations which represents all life on earth, the limits to growth.
If you find yourself asking, “How do we optimize this?”, you are reading them incorrectly. The correct question is: Is the system still permitted to act at all?
4. On Refusal
Refusal is not failure in this framework. It is not silence, cowardice, or conservatism.
Refusal occurs when:
representation collapses
authorization cannot be reconstructed
accountability diffuses beyond addressability
In such cases, action would falsely claim authority. Refusal prevents that claim.

This work expects disagreement. It does not claim to settle debates about intelligence, life, or governance. It claims only that unaccountable authority is viewed as unacceptable, regardless of how sophisticated its source appears to be.
If you disagree with a conclusion but accept the constraints, the resulting framework is doing its job.

argued with

This booklet is a work in progress. The subsequent chapters are not intended to constitute a definitive theory or a comprehensive framework. They are written with the understanding that inquiries regarding authorities, accountabilities, and legitimacies are intricate and cannot thus be conclusively resolved or permanently established. The introductory chapters present thoroughly foundational terms and concepts, but subsequent chapters may undergo modifications, refinements, or even their complete revision. Readers should perceive this textbook as an ongoing exploration rather than a definitive solution.
Definitions are given to help guide discussion, not to end it. Examples are meant to illustrate ideas, not to cover every possibility.
Some arguments are left open on purpose. This is not a mistake, but a way to show that thinking responsibly sometimes means leaving room for doubts and revisions. The goal of this work is now to improve machines that act as moral agents or to automate ethics. It also works to set a clear rule:  systems—whether technical or institutional—should not continue to hold authority if their accountability can no longer be clearly traced to someone who can answer for it.
In this way, the booklet follows its own principle. It stays open to change, interruption, and even rejection.
Part I — The Core Book

The ten chapters and epilogue that state the foundational argument of Harshal's Systems: legitimacy precedes capability, execution may be delegated but legitimacy never migrates, and refusal is the primary act of responsible control.
Formal Distinction — Delegation of Execution vs. Migration of Legitimacy (INV-LEGIT-001): Throughout this work, operational execution may be delegated, but legitimacy never migrates. When a keyed human principal (H(t) = 1 at Center Origin 0•000•000•0000) assigns a bounded task to a machine or sub-agent chain (d = 1..k), only task execution is delegated. The underlying legitimacy remains permanently anchored in the human key. If the human key expires, revokes authorization, or loses addressability, delegated execution halts immediately; no computational component can ever inherit, self-renew, or migrate legitimacy into itself.
