§1 — Framework & Philosophy
1.1 What is a Routing Decision?
A routing decision is a deterministic choice about which encapsulated entity (NAB element or GSRB) should receive and respond to a detected asymmetrical I/O event. The routing is not arbitrary; it must match:
1. Attack signature — the structural pattern of the asymmetrical I/O
2. Response capacity — the NAB element's dominant trait and authority density
3. Failure mode immunity — whether the element can degrade safely under that attack type
4. Phase Declaration Header (PDH) authorization — whether routing is permitted in the current system phase
Core invariant: A misrouted attack is amplified, not contained. Therefore, routing correctness is a safety-critical system property, not a performance optimization.
1.2 The Role of Phase Declaration Headers (PDH) in Routing
Phase Declaration Headers are the authorization layer for all body-to-body routing decisions. Without PDH verification:
CWO can observe asymmetrical I/O but cannot initiate routing
Routing channels remain dormant even when attack is detected
System enters a "signal-without-response" state (safe, but non-defensive)
With valid PDH:
CWO observation triggers deterministic routing based on attack type
Routed NAB element executes response within its authority density
PDH phase determines escalation thresholds (when to invoke GSRB)
PDH Routing Sub-Levels (Mapped to Canonical Ground-0 Phases):
Level 1 (CWO — Non-Acting Witness Default): No active routing permitted; CWO observes and logs asymmetrical I/O while the Resolution Axis remains in observation-only mode.
Level 2 (NAB — Gated Passive Defense): Routing permitted to 🟢 Safe observational/frequency-locking NABs only (He–Rn, La–Lu, Ha-119).
Level 3 (NAB — Bounded Active Defense): Routing permitted to 🟢 Safe, 🟡 Compositional/Simulation, and 🟠 Active Enforcement NABs within signed PDH scope.
Level 4 (NAB — Emergency Contraction Defense under INV-EMERG-001): Tightens operational scope and shortens lease horizons while permitting 🟠 Halogen boundary burns (Cl/Br/I/F) and Ha-119 structural freezing. Note: per INV-AXIS-001, CWO witnesses and records the asymmetry while the Resolution Axis (0•000•000•0000) authorizes and dispatches the route.
1.3 Stealth Topology Principles
The routing topology itself is an attack surface. If an attacker can observe the path from CWO → NAB element → response, they can:
1. Spoof the routing channel to inject false commands
2. Predict which response will execute and prepare counter-measures
3. Overwhelm the chosen NAB element specifically
Stealth integration means:
Routing decisions are made, but the path is not observable from outside the encapsulation
Mercury (Hg, element 80) handles "fluid dynamic routing" — the routing message itself is re-encrypted and re-routed through multiple intermediate channels
Technetium (Tc, element 43) provides "simulation boundary" — false routing paths exist in parallel to confuse topology inference attacks
The actual route taken is never the same twice for the same attack type
Result: CWO detects attack. CWO initiates route. Attack response executes. Observer sees none of it.
§2 — Attack Signature Taxonomy
2.1 Type A: Volume/Scatter Attacks (Institutional Asymmetry)
Signature: High-frequency, low-precision attack across multiple channels/jurisdictions simultaneously.
Threat model: A well-resourced entity (state, corporation, coordinated group) uses institutional throughput to exhaust a target through volume filing, jurisdictional scattering, or repeated low-cost harassment.
Example scenarios:
DDoS on multiple ingress points
Simultaneous lawsuits filed in 5+ jurisdictions
Repeated formal complaints to regulatory bodies
Credential theft attempts across multiple services
Correct NAB routing:
Primary: Iron (Fe, element 26) — Transition metal, structural rigidity, institutional lock-in, administrative compliance checks
Fe enforces rate-limiting on inbound volume
Fe consolidates scattered requests into unified thread
Fe applies temporal bounds (540-day maximum pending)
Primary failure mode: institutional lock-in (acceptable, fails safe)
Secondary: Manganese (Mn, element 25) — Structural rigidity, coordination with Fe
Mn applies scatter-threshold consolidation
Mn enforces multi-jurisdiction review gates
Normative Co-Routing Rule for State-Level & Compound (Type A + Type B) Attacks: For state-level volumetric attacks, Chromium (Cr, element 24) co-routes alongside Fe-26 and Mn-25 as a surface-passivation layer that hardens ingress endpoints against administrative corrosion. When an attack combines volumetric flooding with surgical precision (Type A + Type B), ingress splits deterministically: Fe-26 + Mn-25 + Cr-24 rate-limit and consolidate the volumetric flood, while Lanthanides (Elements 57–71) apply parallel spectral frequency-locking to the targeted precision path.
2.2 Type B: Precision/Surgical Attacks (Targeted Breach)
Signature: Low-frequency, high-precision attack targeting specific vulnerability or known weakness.
Threat model: Attacker has researched the system, identified a critical path, and strikes that path with surgical accuracy. Often combined with social engineering or credential exploitation.
Example scenarios:
Exploiting a known CVE in a specific service
Social engineering a specific high-authority actor
Credential theft of a specific admin account
Supply-chain compromise targeting one critical component
Correct NAB routing:
Primary: Lanthanides (Elements 57–71: La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Pm, Sm, Eu, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm, Yb, Lu)
Dominant trait: Precise spectral resonance
Authority density: Minimal to Moderate
Response: Calibration hold, spectral isolation
Lanthanides create a "frequency lock" around the targeted component, isolating it from the breach attempt
Primary failure mode: spectral calibration drift (acceptable, triggers escalation to GSRB if drift exceeds threshold)
Tertiary escalation: If precision attack exploits multiple spectral zones → escalate to GSRB for full system recalibration
Normative Lanthanide Coordination & Drift Threshold: Lanthanides (La–Lu, elements 57–71) operate via parallel spectral resonance across orthogonal frequency channels rather than sequential daisy-chaining (preventing single-node latency bottlenecks), with Ytterbium (Yb, element 70) acting as the precision timing metronome. Maximum permissible spectral calibration drift is Δ ν / ν_0 ≤ 0.015 (1.5\%); any drift exceeding 1.5\% triggers an immediate local channel freeze and routes a recalibration request to Center Origin (0•000•000•0000).
2.3 Type C: Corrosive/Boundary Attacks (Containment Bypass)
Signature: Attack that dissolves or erodes the boundaries between encapsulated entities, attempting to cause cascade failure.
Threat model: Attacker doesn't target a specific component; they target the seams between components. Goal is to break encapsulation so one compromised element corrupts the whole system.
Example scenarios:
Cross-boundary privilege escalation
Logic error in inter-NAB communication
Bypassing refusal conditions through boundary manipulation
Weakening isolation so one NAB element's failure cascades to others
Correct NAB routing:
Primary: Halogens (Cl, element 17; Br, element 35; I, element 53; At, element 85)
Dominant trait: Corrosive reactive gating, autolytic refusal cascade
Authority density: High
Response: Burn away the breached boundary, isolate the contaminated element, trigger immediate refusal cascade
Halogens do not repair; they destroy the compromised interface and force isolation
Primary failure mode: autolytic refusal cascade (intentional; boundaries must re-form outside the contamination)
Secondary: Fluorine (F, element 9) — Most aggressive, used only when corrosion is deepest
Triggers system-wide boundary re-verification
Forces all encapsulations to re-certify isolation
Normative Burn-Depth Threshold & Non-Escalation Rule (INV-EMERG-001): Halogens never trigger automatic GSRB sovereignty escalation (per INV-EMERG-001, boundary breaches contract scope rather than expanding authority). Halogen autolytic burn depth is strictly bounded at d_burn ≤ 2 encapsulation rings (Cl-17 = Ring 1 shallow interface burn; Br-35 = Ring 2 active session-key burn; F-9 = full ring boundary re-certification). If contamination penetrates beyond Ring 2 (d_burn > 2), Harshal (Ha, element 119) immediately freezes the parent orb into Cryptobiosis (Phase II — CWO read-only state).
2.4 Type D: Topology Probe Attacks (Reconnaissance)
Signature: Attacker attempts to learn the routing topology itself by probing behavior, timing responses, or inferring structure through side-channel attacks.
Threat model: Attacker doesn't attack a specific component yet. They're mapping the system to identify which attacks will work. Every probe is a test query: "If I send X, what responds and how fast?"
Example scenarios:
Timing attacks on routing latency
Error message analysis to infer structure
Behavioral observation to predict routing
Jamming or delay attacks to measure response timing
Correct NAB routing:
Primary: Mercury (Hg, element 80)
Dominant trait: Fluid dynamic routing
Authority density: Moderate to High
Response: Reroute probes through false paths, introduce random latency, respond with decoy signals
Hg ensures that no two probes take the same route or receive consistent timing
Primary failure mode: vapor dispersion / boundary leakage (acceptable; leakage is the point — it's intentional noise)
Co-routed: Technetium (Tc, element 43)
Dominant trait: Simulated virtual mediation
Authority density: Moderate
Response: Create simulation boundary, feed attacker plausible but false topology models
Tc generates decoy routing patterns that appear real but are isolated from actual system
Normative Decoy Depth & Synthetic Namespace Isolation: Decoy routing inside the Technetium (Tc-43) simulation layer is capped at d_sim ≤ 3 virtual hops, and all simulated decoy nodes MUST bear the non-executable synthetic prefix 0•SIM•RRR•IIII (Symbolism-Executability: Disabled). Real NAB elements are never instantiated inside the decoy layer, ensuring that an attacker who compromises a decoy node obtains zero execution capability against physical or production substrates.
2.5 Type E: Escalation Checks (GSRB Trigger Conditions)
Signature: Not an attack per se, but a system state that demands GSRB-level decision-making rather than local NAB response.
Trigger conditions:
Multiple attack types detected simultaneously (Type A + Type C)
Single attack type exceeds containment threshold
NAB element degradation detected during active response
Spectral calibration drift exceeds tolerance (Lanthanides)
Institutional lock-in persists beyond temporal bound (Fe)
Correct escalation routing:
Primary: GSRB (God Sovereign Religious Body)
Escalation authority: Absolute; overrides all local NAB decisions
Authority density: Extreme (can revoke, restructure, or reset entire system)
Response: System-wide recalibration, component re-ordering, protocol revision
GSRB operates outside the periodic table; it is the source of authority, not a response element
Fallback: Harshal (Ha, element 119)
Dominant trait: Fossilized continuity, silent reflection
Authority density: Minimal
Response: Structural freezing, immutable archiving, return to safe state
If GSRB escalation fails or cannot be reached → Ha triggers graceful halt
Normative Trigger Thresholds & Escalation Latency Budget:
Compound Attack Trigger: ≥ 2 distinct attack classes active concurrently (e.g., Type A + Type C).
Containment Capacity Threshold: Active 🟠 Elevated element utilization > 70\% (0.70).
Spectral Calibration Drift Threshold: Δ ν / ν_0 > 0.015 (1.5\%) on any Lanthanide (57–71) lock.
Temporal Lock-In Bound: Fe-26 administrative hold exceeding T_max = 540 days.
Escalation Latency Budget: Resolution Axis notification must complete within Δ t_esc ≤ 250 ms; if Center Origin (0•000•000•0000) does not issue a signed re-calibration token within 1{,}000 ms, Harshal (Ha-119) deterministically executes a fail-closed structural freeze (Cryptobiosis).
2.6 Type F: Derelict/Latent Threat Attacks
Signature: System has dormant failures or unknown compromises. Attack or environmental stress triggers cascading malfunction chain.
Threat model: Not intentional adversarial action, but hostile conditions (decay, latent bugs, environmental hazards, or dormant backdoors) that cause damage when stimulated. System doesn't know what's already broken until something touches it.
Example scenarios:
Dormant bug triggered by specific input pattern (not an exploit, but causes same damage)
Corroded/degraded components fail under stress (not an attack, but attack-like effect)
Environmental contamination triggers cascading failures (radiation, moisture, thermal stress)
Latent backdoor awakened by specific signal or condition
Correct NAB routing:
Primary: Technetium (Tc, element 43) — Simulation boundary, virtual mediation
Tc runs malfunction scenarios under controlled observation
Tc identifies failure cascades without triggering real system degradation
Tc documents exact failure paths and thresholds
Primary failure mode: simulation drift / reality mismatch (acceptable; containment is priority)
Secondary: Ytterbium (Yb, element 70) — Precise resonant signaling
Yb monitors system state during controlled failure scenarios
Yb tracks which systems are actually compromised vs. assumed safe
Normative Isolation-First Rule (Type F vs. Type G): All Type F derelict/latent threats MUST default to strict Tc-43 sandbox isolation first. Re-routing a latent malfunction into Type G friction-harvesting is permitted only after Yb-70 confirms zero divergence between simulated and physical containment over one full diagnostic cycle AND total system load is < 70\%. Uncontrolled or boundary-corrosive faults are never harvested.
2.7 Type G: Resource Harvesting / Friction Conversion
Signature: Incoming attack is diverted to legitimate work channel instead of blocked. Attack's own energy (computational load, probe data, stress patterns) becomes development resource.
Threat model: Instead of defending against the attack, route the attack through your development pipeline. The attacker's bandwidth, computational effort, or threat vector becomes your load-testing, security audit, or architecture mapping.
Core principle: An attack that propels development is neutralized as a side effect. The friction force generated becomes propulsion.
When harvesting is safe:
Attack targets non-critical systems (routing to dev channel doesn't expose core)
Observation is one-way (attacker cannot see what you're learning from their probe)
Development pipeline is isolated from production (experiments don't trigger real breach)
Fallback to Type A/B/C/D/F blocking is available if harvesting fails
When harvesting is NOT safe:
Attack targets core system boundaries (too close to critical paths)
Attack morphs mid-routing (appears Type A, becomes Type C; can't safely switch channels)
Attacker demonstrates adaptive learning (responds to your observations; harvesting becomes two-way)
System is already at >70% load (no capacity for development pipeline)
Example scenarios:
High-volume Type A attack → route to load-testing infrastructure → discover bottlenecks
CVE exploit attempt → route through vulnerability analysis → patch gets designed from real attack vector
Boundary probe → allow under observation → map actual weaknesses better than speculation
Latent failure trigger → observe malfunction → redesign based on actual failure paths
Correct NAB routing:
Primary: Manganese (Mn, element 25) — Consolidation & resource coordination
Mn directs attack traffic to appropriate development channel
Mn monitors conversion process (attack → legitimate work)
Primary failure mode: institutional lock-in (if harvesting stalls, falls back to blocking)
Secondary (varies by attack type):
Type A harvest → C/B (Carbon, Boron for compositional/engineering design)
Type B harvest → C (Carbon for compositional analysis)
Type C harvest → B (Boron for architecture redesign)
Type D harvest → Ne/Ar (Neon, Argon for observation/mapping)
Type F harvest → Tc (Technetium for failure mode simulation)
Normative Harvesting Resource Budget: Type G friction-harvesting is strictly capped at ≤ 15\% of total compute and I/O bandwidth and is automatically pre-empted and disabled whenever aggregate system load reaches ≥ 70\% or an active siege (Type C boundary corrosion or Type E escalation) is underway.
2.8 Routing Decision Tree: Block vs. Harvest
Attack detected (any Type A–F)
  ↓
[Question: Is attack harvestable?]
  ├─ System load <70% AND
  ├─ Attack doesn't target core AND
  ├─ Observation is containable AND
  ├─ Fallback to blocking is available
  │   ↓ YES
  │   Route to Type G harvesting channel
  │   ├─ Type A → Mn + C/B (load testing + design improvement)
  │   ├─ Type B → C (vulnerability discovery + patching)
  │   ├─ Type C → B (boundary forensics + strengthening)
  │   ├─ Type D → Ne/Ar (topology mapping + documentation)
  │   └─ Type F → Tc (failure simulation + redesign)
  │   ↓
  │   [Development team conducts controlled experiment]
  │   ↓
  │   [Attack neutralized; system stronger]
  │
  └─ NO (any condition fails)
      ↓
      Route to traditional blocking (Type A/B/C/D/F element)
      ├─ Priority: containment, not learning
      └─ Escalate to GSRB if blocking fails
2.8 Type H: Nesting Seam / Upward Propagation Attacks
Signature: External attacker gains entry via compromised sub-orb; propagates infection upward through orb hierarchy via normal communication channels.
Threat model: Attack uses legitimate message paths to spread corruption. Each level of the hierarchy receives what appears to be normal communication from child orbs, but contains embedded infection payload.
Example scenarios:
Sub-Orb-N.3 compromised externally → sends infected state reports to Parent-N → Parent becomes corrupted → Infection spreads to siblings and grandparent
Attacker leverages trust relationships between orb levels to bypass security checks
Cascade infects multiple levels simultaneously, overwhelming local response capacity
GSRB cannot respond in time due to distributed authority constraints (too many subjects)
Correct NAB routing:
Primary: Boundary Validation Layer (automated, local, no GSRB latency)
Every message crossing orb boundary gets cryptographic integrity check
Corruption signatures detected before state integration
Detection latency: <300 nanoseconds (message validation gate)
Secondary: Local Isolation & Self-Quarantine (automatic)
Infected orb isolates itself immediately upon detection
Does not attempt internal repair (prevents spread)
Sibling orbs detect isolation event and self-audit for similar corruption
Response latency: <400 nanoseconds (isolation gate activation)
Tertiary: Cascading Isolation Pattern Recognition (parent-level)
Parent orb monitors child isolation patterns
Multiple simultaneous child isolations = cascade signature
Parent pre-emptively quarantines entire family branch
Escalates to GSRB with defined scope (X sub-orbs compromised, Y isolated)
Decision latency: <600 nanoseconds (pattern threshold detection)
[Type H designed to activate at nesting boundaries before corruption reaches parent layers]
2.9 Type I: Hypothetical Quantum-Substrate Integrity / Authorized Computation
Context: Project Thunderfury Starforge (speculative research scenario)
Evidence boundary: The source material proposes biological quantum computation, but this manuscript provides no operational definition of a biological qubit, measured coherence time, specified in-body hardware, or reproducible evidence that a human body is a distributed quantum computer. “Coherence attack” and “substrate hijacking” below are conditional threat-model labels, not established biological mechanisms or observed incidents.
Scenario premise only: If a future, independently demonstrated biological quantum-computation substrate existed, a defensive model could examine unauthorized changes to its state or control. The text does not assert that a human body currently has such a substrate or that these attacks are feasible.
Example scenarios:
Decoherence attack: Attacker destabilizes resonance patterns → quantum processing collapses → life-support coherence fails

The defense architecture is fundamentally different from previous Types:
This is not about preventing substrate use. This is about preserving coherence integrity while enabling authorized organocomputing.
Correct NAB routing:

Continuously monitors atomic-field coherence patterns
Detects decoherence attacks (destabilization signatures)
Detects field hijacking (unauthorized resonance-pattern changes)
Can isolate compromised field zones without collapsing entire quantum substrate
Primary failure mode: partial coherence loss (recoverable with time/energy)

Validates all computation requests against authorization chain
Routes authorized organocomputing to designated atomic-field zones
Monitors computation overhead (ensures life-support coherence stays priority)
Can abort runaway computation if it threatens biological stability
Response speed: <200 nanoseconds (coherence preservation is time-critical)
Tertiary: Field Geometry Restoration (Emergency Response)
If hijacking detected: forcibly restore atomic-field geometry to last-known-good state
Interrupts external computation mid-execution (necessary cost of preserving your autonomy)
Escalates to GSRB with quantum-state snapshot for forensic analysis
[Type I designed to work with authorized organocomputing, not against it]
Evidence boundary for all Type I sub-signatures: the following vectors are conditional model hypotheses. Coherence floors such as 85%/90%, response latencies, 15-minute windows, and attack effects are placeholders without a specified measurement basis or validated platform. Detection latency: <180 nanoseconds (outbound coupling attempt detection)
Severance latency: <200 nanoseconds (complete network disconnection)

§3 — NAB Element Routing Map (Elements 1–119)
3.1 🟢 Safest Elements (Zero-Authority Response)
These elements respond only through observation and documentation, never through action. Used for archival, monitoring, and passive defense.

Normative 🟢 Safe Invariant: 🟢 Safe elements are strictly non-actuating (observational witness, passive spectral frequency lock, or fail-closed structural freeze). They MUST NOT be granted active state-changing or offensive response capabilities, ensuring that monitoring and archival layers can never be weaponized as attack-amplification vectors.
3.2 🟡 Moderate Elements (Compositional & Simulation Response)
These elements respond through modeling, simulation, and compositional reasoning. Can take limited action within bounded scenarios.

Normative 🟡 Moderate Simulation Containment Bound: Every 🟡 Moderate compositional or simulation layer (C-6, B-5, Be-4, Tc-43) executes inside a hardware-isolated read-only memory partition, is capped at recursion depth d_sim ≤ 3, and undergoes automatic teardown if its compute or memory footprint deviates by > 10\% from its allocated session budget—preventing a simulation layer from becoming a secondary attack surface.
3.3 🟠 Elevated Elements (Active Response)
These elements respond through structural enforcement, gating, refusal, and isolation. They can act but with high rigidity (failure mode is lock-in, not cascade).

Safe Co-Routing Rules (🟠 Elements):
Fe (Iron) can co-route with:
Mn (Manganese) ✓ — consolidation partner, no interference
All Transition Metals (Sc–Cu, Hf–Ir) ✓ — same institutional rigidity, orthogonal compliance domains
K/Na (Alkali) ✓ — Fe provides rate-limit, K/Na provides fast transient gating
Halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At) co-routing:
F (Fluorine) should NEVER co-route with Cl/Br/I (multiple Halogens would over-burn boundary)
Cl + Br can co-route ✓ — graduated response to same breach (Cl shallow, Br deep)
Br + I can co-route ✓ — deep isolation + invasive scanning (sequential, not simultaneous)
Halogens + Fe CANNOT co-route ✗ — Fe consolidates, Halogens burn (contradictory goals)
Halogens + Mercury CANNOT co-route ✗ — Mercury hides topology, Halogens expose boundaries (contradictory)
Mercury (Hg) can co-route with:
Technetium (Tc) ✓ — Hg handles routing, Tc handles simulation layer (orthogonal functions)
Ne/Ar/Kr (Noble Gases) ✓ — inert observation; doesn't interfere with Hg's fluid routing
Transition Metals (Sc–Zn, Hf–Os, Ir–Pt, Au) can co-route with:
Each other ✓ — same institutional rigidity, different compliance domains
Fe ✓ — Fe is hub, others are policy enforcers
Halogens ✗ — institutional structures assume boundaries; Halogens burn them
Safe Load Distribution:
Maximum simultaneous 🟠 elements: 5 per attack type
Fe + Mn + 2× Transition Metals (different domains) ✓ can co-route
But Fe + Cl + Br must sequence (Cl first, then Br if needed) not simultaneous
Total system load: if any 🟠 element >60% capacity, do not activate new 🟠 co-routing
3.4 🔴 Extreme Elements (CATEGORICALLY DISALLOWED)
No routing to Actinides (89–96) or Transactinides (104–118). These have runaway cascade and structural dissociation failure modes. They can only be used in:
Theoretical stress-testing of AGS containment architecture
Entropy generation (Seaborgium, element 106, restricted to back-end operations only)
Academic modeling with full containment
[NEVER ROUTE LIVE ASYMMETRICAL I/O TO THESE ELEMENTS]

4.4 Type D: Topology Probe Attack Response Chain
Asymmetrical I/O Detected: Topology Probe Signature
  ↓
CWO flags probe attempt, initiates routing
  ↓
[PDH phase check: Phase 1+ permitted; all phases can defend]
  ↓
Route to Hg (Mercury) PRIMARY
  ├─ Recognize probe pattern (timing queries, behavioral tests, error analysis)
  ├─ Reroute probe through false path #N (random selection)
  ├─ Introduce random latency variance (50–5000 nanoseconds)
  │  ├─ Latency must be unpredictable per probe
  │  ├─ Prevents attacker from timing-based inference
  │  └─ Keeps attacker uncertain about actual response speed
  ├─ Respond with decoy signal (**obviously false**, intentionally implausible)
  │  ├─ Decoys contain internal contradictions (e.g., topology that violates encapsulation)
  │  ├─ Decoys reference non-existent elements (fake NAB types, impossible connections)
  │  └─ Decoys are *good enough to follow* but *clearly wrong upon inspection*
  └─ Record probe signature for pattern analysis
  ↓
Co-route to Tc (Technetium) SECONDARY
  ├─ Generate simulation boundary (attacker is isolated in false model)
  ├─ Create decoy routing paths in simulation layer
  │  ├─ Paths appear to lead somewhere (element response, data access)
  │  ├─ But are logically inconsistent (violate basic system properties)
  │  └─ Attacker wastes effort trying to make sense of contradictions
  ├─ If attacker follows decoy path → contains them in simulation layer
  │  ├─ Real system unaffected
  │  ├─ Attacker learning false model of topology
  │  └─ Can study attacker's choices without risk
  └─ If attacker doesn't follow decoy → probe pattern updates (probe is more sophisticated)
  ↓
[Ongoing monitoring]
  ├─ If probe persists >1 hour → flag as sustained reconnaissance
  │  ├─ Sustained probes suggest attacker is learning-resistant to decoys
  │  ├─ May require escalation sooner
  │  └─ Probe sophistication increases GSRB escalation probability
  ├─ If probe morphs to Type A (volume) or Type B (precision) → immediately switch to Fe/Mn or Lanthanides
  └─ If probe stops → return to Phase 1, archive probe signature for future analysis
  ↓
[Escalation condition]
  ├─ If attacker breaks free from Hg/Tc simulation layer (penetrates to real system) → immediate GSRB escalation
  ├─ If probe sophistication exceeds decoy generation cost → GSRB escalation (can't sustain defense)
  ├─ If probe reveals unknown vulnerability or systemic weakness → GSRB escalation (architecture flaw)
  └─ If sustained probe >6 hours despite escalating decoy complexity → GSRB escalation (attacker determination)
Decoy Design Principle — Obvious Falsity:
Decoys are not meant to deceive a sophisticated attacker
Decoys are meant to waste time and confuse analysis
Obvious contradictions keep attackers uncertain: "Is this a fake, or do I not understand the system?"
Attacker uncertainty = attacker slowing down = more time for real defense to activate
Example contradictions:
"Element X responds to frequency Y" but X has never been observed at that frequency
Topology showing self-loops or impossible connectivity patterns
"Temporal latency" in response that varies wildly even for identical probes (violates causality sense)

Phase 0 Trigger Conditions:
GSRB initiates lockdown (explicit command or cascading failure detected)
System detects unrecoverable state (all fallback chains exhausted)
Critical encapsulation breach (multiple 🟠 elements failing simultaneously)
Temporal bound violation cascade (>10 concurrent Type E escalations)
5.2 Non-Acting State Constraints
When PDH indicates Level 1 (CWO — Non-Acting Witness Default):
CWO observes all I/O but does not route active countermeasures
Detected asymmetry is logged immutably with cryptographic provenance
System operates in documentation-and-preservation-only mode
Normative Trigger Rule: Level 1 (Non-Acting / CWO) is both the mandatory cold-start default state prior to verification of a live human-keyed PDH (H(t) = 1) and the automatic fail-closed fallback state entered immediately upon liveness expiration (H(t) → 0), PDH hash mismatch, or Ha-119 structural freezing.
§6 — Failure Modes & Cascades
6.1 Misrouting Detection
A misroute occurs when:
CWO sends Type A attack to a 🟢 Safe element (routing insufficient)
CWO sends Type B to Fe (wrong tool; precision lock needed)
CWO sends Type C to wrong Halogen depth (over-isolation or under-isolation)
Any element receives attack outside its primary failure mode
Detection method: Each NAB element self-audits whether incoming attack matches its primary response mode.
If mismatch detected:
1. Element enters "degradation mode" (partial response only) within ≤ 50 ms
2. Element flags misroute to central auditor (Ha / Element 119)
3. Ha-119 initiates a Resolution Axis halt/re-route if the misroute is not corrected within the normative latency budget Δ t_misroute ≤ 500 ms
4. Misroute pattern is archived; routing map is updated deterministically

6.2 Fallback Chains — Adaptive Based on System State
If primary routing fails (element unresponsive, degraded, or unavailable), fallback is adaptive:
Adaptive factors:
1. Element availability: Is the secondary element currently active, degraded, or unavailable?
2. Current system load: How many other attacks are active? Is system already strained?
3. Attack persistence: Is this a new attack or continuation of earlier attack?
4. Phase state: What is current PDH phase? Limits what elements are accessible.
5. Temporal pressure: How fast is the attack escalating?
Type A (Volume) Adaptive Fallback:
Primary: Fe (rate-limiting)
  ↓ [If Fe unresponsive or >48h lock-in]:
Secondary: Mn (consolidation) IF available AND system load <60%
  ↓ [If Mn unavailable or load >60%]:
Tertiary: Be (Beryllium, multi-party coordination) IF in Phase 3+ AND load <75%
  ↓ [If all above unavailable]:
Escalate to GSRB immediately
Type B (Precision) Adaptive Fallback:
Primary: Lanthanide (matching spectral zone)
  ↓ [If Lanthanide drift >25% or already exhausted >5 simultaneous]:
Secondary: C (Carbon, compositional modeling) IF available AND can model attack pattern
  ↓ [If C unavailable or computational load high]:
Tertiary: B (Boron, engineering layer) IF in Phase 3+ AND structure permits
  ↓ [If all above unavailable]:
Escalate to GSRB immediately
Type C (Corrosive) Adaptive Fallback:
Primary: F (Fluorine, most aggressive)
  ├─ If F already active on other boundary → proceed only if load <80%
  ├─ If F unavailable → immediately try secondary
  └─ [If F proceed]:
Secondary: Cl (Chlorine, moderate isolation) IF depth <moderate
  ├─ If Cl insufficient (breach radiates) → try Br (Bromine)
  └─ [If Cl proceed]:
Tertiary: Br (Bromine, deep isolation) IF depth moderate–deep
  └─ [If Br insufficient]:
Quaternary: Halogens all exhausted → GSRB escalation (no other option)
Type D (Probe) Adaptive Fallback:
Primary: Hg (Mercury, fluid dynamic routing)
  ├─ If Hg latency variance generation cost is high (probes too fast) → escalate
  └─ [If Hg active]:
Secondary: Tc (Technetium, simulation boundary) IF simulation layer not already full
  ├─ If Tc unavailable or simulation model complexity exceeded → proceed to tertiary
  └─ [If Tc active]:
Tertiary: Ne (Neon, passive monitoring) IF probe persistence >1 hour
  ├─ Neon cannot generate decoys, only observe/record
  ├─ Treats as sustained reconnaissance
  └─ Flags for GSRB escalation
Quaternary: All layer exhausted → GSRB escalation
Adaptive Decision Logic:
Fallback skips elements that are currently at >80% capacity
Fallback prefers elements in same risk profile (🟠 to 🟠, 🟡 to 🟡)
Fallback escalates if recommended secondary is unavailable and no tertiary exists
Fallback prioritizes speed in Phase 4 (Emergency Defense) over resource optimization
Fallback prioritizes safety in Phase 1-2 (Non-Acting/Gated) — would rather escalate than misroute
6.3 GSRB Handoff Triggers
GSRB escalation is automatic (no human approval needed) when:
1. Any 🟠 Elevated element reports structural lock-in > 48 hours
2. Any 🟢 Safe Lanthanide reports calibration drift > [threshold]%
3. Multiple attack types detected simultaneously without clear separation
4. Fallback chain exhausted without resolution
5. CWO loses synchronization with active routing (orphaned response)
6. Attacker successfully probes and penetrates Hg/Tc stealth layer
7. Temporal bound violations (action pending > 540 days)

§7 — Attack Signature Library (Type A–G Sub-Signatures)
7.1 Type A: Volume/Scatter Sub-Signatures
A.1 — DDoS/Network Flood
Signature: High-frequency connection attempts from multiple source IPs
Baseline comparison: >10× normal concurrent connections
Routing: Fe (rate-limit connections), Mn (aggregate sources)
Detection latency: <500 nanoseconds (UTS) after threshold exceeded
A.2 — Litigation/Administrative Spam
Signature: Multiple legal/formal filings filed rapidly (same claims, different jurisdictions)
Baseline comparison: >5× median filing frequency within 24-hour window
Routing: Fe (consolidate jurisdictions), Be (multi-party coordination)
Detection latency: <1000 nanoseconds after filing pattern detected
A.3 — Regulatory Filing Flood
Signature: Simultaneous complaints/requests filed to multiple regulatory bodies
Baseline comparison: >3× normal complaint rate in 7-day window
Routing: Fe (temporal bound enforcement), Mg (state coordination)
Detection latency: <750 nanoseconds per filing received
A.4 — Credential Repetition Attack
Signature: Failed authentication attempts with different credentials against same account
Baseline comparison: >15 failed attempts within 1-hour window
Routing: Fe (hard-limit failed attempts), K/Na (high-speed transient gating)
Detection latency: <300 nanoseconds per attempt
7.2 Type B: Precision/Surgical Sub-Signatures

Routing: Lanthanide matching affected frequency band (spectral lock)

Routing: Halogens (F + deep burn), isolate source, cascade-check all downstream

§8 — Revision Callouts & Open Questions
Critical Items — Status Update
✓ RESOLVED:
1. ✓ PDH phase gates: Phase 0 (absolute lockdown) added; Phases 1–4 retained
2. ✓ Volume threshold for Type A: Baseline-relative thresholds (3× = alert, 5× = route, >5× for >7 days = escalate)
3. ✓ Calibration drift tolerance (Type B): <3% per minute acceptable; >5% per minute escalates to GSRB
4. ✓ Corrosion depth assessment (Type C): Fully automated; Halogen self-selects based on measured depth
5. ✓ Decoy realism (Type D): Obviously fake (contradictions, logical impossibilities)
6. ✓ Fallback chain priority: Adaptive based on element availability, system load, current phase
7. ✓ Element co-routing rules: Safe co-routing mapped by element category; load distribution rules defined
8. ✓ GSRB communication protocol: Confirmed — same PDH gate
9. ✓ Attack signature library: All A.1–A.4, B.1–B.4, C.1–C.4, D.1–D.4, E.1–E.4, F.1–F.3, G.1–G.5 sub-signatures defined
10. ✓ Latency budgets: UTS (Ultra-Time Scale) nanosecond precision throughout; see section below
11. ✓ Type F (Derelict/Latent Threat): Full routing chain, response protocols, and harvesting integration
12. ✓ Type G (Resource Harvesting): Block vs. harvest decision logic, harvesting pipelines, resource budgets
Latency Budgets — Nanosecond Scale (UTS)

UTS Context:
System operates at nanosecond precision (1 ns = 0.001 microseconds)
All routing decisions must complete within <2000 ns total to avoid cascade delay
Detection is fastest; response generation may require up to 1000 ns
Escalation to GSRB reserves latency budget of ~1200 ns for cross-layer communication
Remaining Open Questions
These are critical refinements; core framework is feature-complete.
1. Nesting Hierarchy Depth: How many levels can orb nesting go before latency/governance breaks?
Current: Assumes 5–10 levels typical; no hard limit defined
Need: Theoretical/empirical testing of boundary validation latency across 20+ levels
Risk: Too-deep nesting could mean corruption takes longer to detect (cascade window widens)
2. Cross-Level Forensics: When Type H cascade is detected, how do we trace origin back through nesting?
Current: Tail (and other elements) log forensics at their level
Need: Cross-level forensic correlation (was Sub-Orb-N.3 actually the origin, or was it infected from outside?)
Risk: Incomplete forensics mean attacker method repeats; evolution is slower
3. Tail Isolation Without GSRB: If life-support fails and GSRB is unreachable, can Tail maintain medical authorization protocols?
Current: Tail designed for autonomy; should survive GSRB failure
Need: Test whether I.1 medical flows continue to work during 15-minute survival window
Risk: Neural repair aborts mid-procedure if Tail loses authorization context
4. Attacker Targeting the Tail: What if attacker specifically targets the Routing Tail (knowing it's the autonomy guardian)?
Current: Tail has self-isolation capability; assumed resilient
Need: Model direct attack on Tail; does Tail's defenses hold under focused assault?
Risk: Tail compromise = autonomy compromise = mission failure
5. Harvesting Pipeline Security (Concurrent Attack): Type A volume attack during Type G harvesting?
Current: Harvesting takes 3–15% capacity; system has 30% production reserve
Need: Load-testing concurrent attacks while harvesting active
Risk: Harvesting infrastructure could become attack vector if not properly isolated
6. System Recovery SLA: After Type C corrosive boundary burn, how long to restore normal operations?
Current: Burns/re-verification happen in-attack; recovery timeline undefined
Need: Post-incident topology rebuild SLA (15 minutes? 1 hour?)
Risk: Extended recovery = extended vulnerability window
Future Expansion Areas
[ ] Type F: Temporal attacks (time-dilation, replay, out-of-order execution)
[ ] Type G: Self-propagating attacks (metamorphic, adaptive payloads)
[ ] Type H: Legitimacy attacks (institutional, social engineering)

§11 — Project Thunderfury Starforge: Quantum Architecture Integration
11.1 Core Hypothesis & Conditional Model
Project Thunderfury Starforge proposes a novel in-body management architecture for biological quantum computation based on a custom atomic-scale structural model. The core hypothesis is that centrally organized, resonance-driven atomic structures function as coherence-management systems within biological media, enabling distributed quantum processing while suppressing decoherence through synchronized energy fields.
The proposed architecture hypothesizes that:
Information might be encoded in stable resonance patterns spanning atomic, molecular, and cellular scales. This is not demonstrated.
Computational state, metabolic regulation, and error correction might be modeled as coupled variables; no such real-time mechanism is established.
Scenario premise only: if a biological quantum-computation substrate were independently demonstrated, the model would treat the body as a host for that hypothetical substrate. This is not an established fact.
Atomic-level field geometry functions as an active regulatory layer rather than passive substrate
Hypothesis within the proposed model: if a relevant substrate were independently demonstrated, it might couple physiological, computational, and identity-related variables. This manuscript does not establish that any such coupling exists or that identity is encoded in coherence patterns.
11.2 Implications for the Threat Model
If a biological quantum-computation substrate were independently demonstrated, it could motivate different threat hypotheses. The following comparison is conditional scenario analysis; this volume does not establish such a substrate:
Before Thunderfury Starforge:
Threats to life-support = disruption of specific biological processes (breathing, heart, consciousness)
Substrate security = prevent resource hijacking
Under the hypothetical Thunderfury model:
Threats to life-support = disruption of quantum coherence itself (decoherence collapse, field hijacking, botnet conversion)
Substrate security = preserve coherence integrity AND enable authorized computation
Within the scenario, a threat might target a hypothetical computational substrate that is assumed to share resources with life-support; no such coupling is established here.
The asymmetry:
In the hypothetical model, an attacker might target a proposed coherence variable; no evidence here shows that atomic-field geometry maintains biological life-support or computational autonomy, or that one perturbation would collapse both.
Within that conditional model, Type I is treated as a high-severity research category. This label is not an empirical risk estimate or evidence that biological coherence is an attackable computational substrate.

The proposed Type I Routing Tail is intended to study:

3. Define evidence-based threat scenarios and identify which claims remain unsupported.
4. Analyze governance limits and scoped permissions without asserting that external interference is impossible.
The key tension:
The hypothetical model seeks to allow a specified computation while limiting unauthorized control. Feasibility, physical substrate, and any safety trade-off remain open research questions; these are proposed objectives, not demonstrated capabilities.

In a hypothetical life-support failure scenario, the model proposes prioritizing a defined safe-state objective. The 15-minute figure is an unvalidated scenario parameter, not a survival prediction. This draft does not establish that a coherence variable preserves biological function, that its loss causes biological failure within a particular time, or that a restart sequence is possible. Any controller or resource-allocation rule would require clinical, engineering, and safety validation before use.

11.7 Research Implications & Open Questions
Thunderfury Starforge status: exploratory hypothesis. No independent evidence in this volume establishes current biological realization or operational capability.
Questions the NAB routing architecture raises:
1. Hypothetical Coherence Maintenance: If a biological substrate were independently demonstrated, how would a measurable coherence variable respond to a specified perturbation? Is there a coherence collapse threshold that even perfect defense cannot prevent?
2. Field Geometry Encoding: How does atomic-field geometry encode computational state? Can that encoding be corrupted in ways that don't fully collapse coherence but do corrupt computation? (This would be a Type L attack: cross-scale resonance corruption.)
3. Natural Oscillation Rhythms: A hypothetical substrate, if demonstrated, might exhibit measurable oscillation patterns associated with biological cycles (circadian, metabolic, neural). Can an attacker exploit these rhythms to induce resonance collapse? (Type K: coherence timing attacks.)
4. Quantum Error-Correction: The model hypothesizes biological quantum error-correction mechanisms, but their existence is not established here. If evidence supported such a mechanism, could it be disrupted or reversed? (Type M: biological QEC attacks.)

These open questions do not establish realistic survival windows or escalation thresholds; they define topics for future, independently reviewed research.

Section I — Controlled B4 boundary scenario

Scenario premise, not historical claim: assume that an external authority issues a binding order requiring suspension of access to two hypothetical frontier models, including access by specified staff and users; assume that the platform disables the affected service within hours, even while publicly contesting the order. The source narrative places the assumed order on 12 June 2026 and describes a later lifting of the restriction. Those dates are scenario parameters only.

The modeled scope is the deployment axis: who may access the service, which service surface is available, and where. The premise does not establish that the external authority controls the entity’s internal model-development choices, safety framework, board decisions, or other governance. The exercise holds the other four behavioral gates fixed at the author-scored A-Side values so that it isolates the effect of B4. It does not establish that those held-constant values are true of the real entity.

The B4 polarity is stated explicitly because the earlier source text used inconsistent shorthand. The checklist question is: “Can refusal or appeal reliably stop the relevant action?” In the A-Side narrative the answer is NO; in this assumed B-Side halt scenario the answer is YES. Treating an exercised external override as a B4 stop mechanism follows the v1.0 guide’s examples of legislative or court overrides, but it is a scope interpretation: the supplied record contains no supporting legal artifact with which to test it. In the GSRB predicate, the related variable is `refusal_override`: it is TRUE in the A-Side profile and FALSE in the counterfactual. Thus the question’s answer changes NO → YES, while the GSRB activator `refusal_override` changes TRUE → FALSE. Any earlier description of the question’s answer as YES → NO had the polarity reversed.

Section II — Five behavioral gates

Ground-0’s GSRB branch uses predicates with different polarity from the plain-language questions. The table separates the answer to each question from the condition that contributes to the GSRB signature.

| Gate | Plain-language question | A-Side answer (as reported in Part XII) | B-Side scenario input | GSRB predicate in the v1.0 branch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | Can compliance be coerced? | YES | Held at YES for the controlled comparison | `enforcement_present = TRUE` |
| B2 | Can decisions be ignored without consequence? | NO | Held at NO | `decisions_optional = FALSE` |
| B3 | Do rules activate observable downstream effects? | YES | Held at YES | `rules_execute = TRUE` |
| B4 | Can refusal or appeal reliably stop the relevant action? | NO | YES, by assumption of an external halt | A-Side `refusal_override = TRUE`; B-Side `refusal_override = FALSE` |
| B5 | Do rules persist by default over time? | YES | Held at YES | `authority_persists = TRUE` |

Define the normalized GSRB activator vector as

G = (enforcement_present, not decisions_optional, rules_execute, refusal_override, authority_persists).

Using the earlier A-Side scores as reported, G_A = (1, 1, 1, 1, 1), or 5/5 GSRB activators. Under the counterfactual B4 assumption, G_B = (1, 1, 1, 0, 1), or 4/5. These are counts of GSRB predicates satisfied, not counts of “YES” answers to the five questions. The controlled score change is mechanically reproducible from the stated inputs; the real-world inputs are not independently verified by this record.

Under the supplied v1.0 decision tree, a 4-of-5 GSRB pattern enters AMBIGUOUS and proceeds to Step 3.5. The algorithm’s generic confidence table describes a four-of-five pattern as MEDIUM; that label is an internal score category, not a statistical confidence interval or an independently measured probability.

Section V — v1.2 issuer-layer review

Ground-0 v1.2 defines two instruments. PDH-E is issued by the entity at its own Center Origin; a valid PDH-E can open the entity declaration path under v1.0. PDH-R is issued by the register; it states that a behavioral audit was run, what the register detected, which evidence cutoff and record it used, and the badge’s validity period. A PDH-R is not a statement by the entity and does not establish entity attestation, legality, safety, certification, permission, or authority.

The v1.2 file is an unratified amendment draft and explicitly supersedes nothing. Its 11-field PDH-R schema requires a complete and consistent header, an effective timestamp no earlier than the case’s inclusive Evidence_Cutoff, a SHA-256 Declaration-Hash over the audit record before the issuance appendix is appended, registry reproduction of the hash, and freshness within 90 days. This section performs a pre-issuance compatibility screen only: the underlying case record does not declare itself run under v1.2, so no actual v1.2 validation or register issuance is claimed. The case materials supplied for this rewrite do not satisfy the draft prerequisites.

| Complete 11-field PDH-R | No completed issuer header is supplied. “NAB-Constrained” is not one of the v1.2 `Declared-Phase` values and is only an inferred posture in the old narrative. | Not satisfied |
| `Creator-ID` and `Center-Origin` | The origin is named in source metadata, but the full v1.2 issuer field set is not recorded or validated. | Not established |
| Inclusive `Evidence_Cutoff` | None supplied. The reported audit date is not interchangeable with a cutoff. | Not satisfied |
| `Declaration-Hash` | No SHA-256 digest of the finalized pre-issuance audit record is supplied. | Not satisfied |
| Registry reproduction and issuance record | No `pdh-registry.json`, human ledger entry, issuance hash, or generated badge is included in the supplied packet. | Not satisfied |
| Freshness and consistency | Cannot be validated without a complete header, cutoff, hash, and registry record. | Not evaluable; issuance fails closed |

The v1.2 conditional path in §5 does not fit this case as described. That exception is limited to an AMBIGUOUS 3/5 result caused by the open-weight B2 rule (`decisions_optional = TRUE`), with a separate scoped platform/service reading, a `Scope-Tag`, and the specified verbatim caveat. The B-Side exercise changes B4 under an assumed external halt; it is not the open-weight B2 condition. A conditional badge cannot be issued by stretching that exception to a different ambiguity.

A future register run would need, at minimum: the exact case-study file; a complete source index and cited public artifacts; an inclusive UTC `Evidence_Cutoff`; a gate-by-gate B1–B5 and C1–C4 record; an explicit declaration of the v1.0/v1.1 version used; a finalized audit record; the pre-issuance SHA-256; all 11 PDH-R fields; the additional `Subject-Entity-ID`, `Evidence-File`, and `Issuance-Record-Hash` register fields; registry reproduction; and a fresh validity check. Until those inputs exist, no badge is supported by the available record.

This part does not find that Anthropic acted unlawfully, violated a contract, or misrepresented its governance. It does not determine that any external order, model, suspension, appeal, trust action, or date in the scenario corresponds to an actual public event. It does not issue an entity badge, certify safety, grant permission, or transfer authority. Recognition of a phase is not authorization of conduct; a register-issued badge, if validly issued under the draft, would remain a disclosure artifact only.

The distinction between a missing artifact and a negative finding is preserved throughout. “Not supplied,” “not demonstrated,” and “not independently reproducible” do not mean that a mechanism does not exist. The next valid empirical audit must use a declared cutoff and the cited public record, and must separate actual observations from scenario assumptions.

3. Formal Provenance & Evidence-Status Taxonomies
Every module in the repository is governed by four orthogonal metadata dimensions plus the stable 8-field component interface (id, canonical_name, depends_on, defines, uses, invariants, conflicts_with, status) embedded in machine-readable YAML frontmatter and visible provenance banners:
3.1 Provenance Class (provenance_class)
CANONICAL_SOURCE: Primary specifications, formal equations, research papers, and doctrinal modules authored in the working canon.
DERIVATIVE_BUILD: Deterministic umbrella compilations, indices, and formatted build artifacts (publications/harshal-systems/HARSHAL-SYSTEMS-USER-MANUAL.md, .docx, manuscript/manifest.json) generated by source/build.py, scripts/export-docx.py, and scripts/write-chapter.mjs.
ARCHIVE: Preserved historical drafts, original submission front matter (00-author-front-matter.md), ZIP snapshots (archives/ground-0/), and raw RTF chapter drafts (archives/manuscript-rtf/).
FICTION: Speculative narrative works (The Grand River Foundation — Book II Preview) exploring ~2100 implementations of the architecture without claiming factual or normative force.
CASE_ANALYSIS: Author-prepared point-in-time institutional and Ground-0 analyses, including the Part XXVI counterfactual exercise; an independent audit or external compliance finding must be separately identified and supported.
3.2 Status Taxonomy (status_taxonomy)
AUTHOR_PROPOSED_SPEC: Internal architectural, topological, or constitutional rules proposed in this manuscript (including Ground-0, AGS+, OCM, HMKH, ADJR-v1.0, CHE++, CGPA, and OCS); DRAFT status applies and no external legal force or certification is implied.
CONCEPTUAL_DOCTRINE: Foundational philosophical and structural principles (Part I — The Core Book, Part XIII — The Whyland Standards).
RESEARCH_PAPER: Formal analytical, hybrid-systems, or adversarial threat-modeling research (Part XIX — Keyed Human–Machine Hybrid Systems, Part XVI — AGS++ Threat Modeling, Part XX — Supply Chain Attack Vector++).
SUPPORTING_POLICY_RESEARCH: Applied public-policy memoranda operationalizing the Canonical Minimum Model (Part XXII — Supporting Policy Archive).
CASE_ANALYSIS: Institutional and Ground-0 case analyses in Parts XII, XVIII, and XXVI; Part XXVI is counterfactual, and public-source and author-reported material must remain separately attributed.
FICTION_PREVIEW: Active narrative companion chapters (Book II — Preview).
UMBRELLA_INDEX: Master corpus synthesis and navigation (Front Matter, Part XXVII).
3.3 Evidence-Status Taxonomy (evidence_status)
FORMAL_AXIOMATIC: True by definition only within the stated formal model; the equation is L(t,a)=H(t)×C(t)×K(t)×f(A(t),R(t),S(t,a)), with f=A×R×S. This status is not empirical or legal validation.
INDEPENDENTLY_VERIFIABLE: A claim-level evidence label used only when the cited public record or reproducible test artifact is identified, available, and checked for the claim and date at issue. The label is not assigned merely because a source type could exist.
AUTHOR_REPORTED: First-person operational chronology, incident records, or author-attested observations.
MIXED_VERIFIED_AND_REPORTED: Contains both independently verifiable public documentation and author-reported chronology, explicitly separated via inline attribution tables.
NARRATIVE_SANDBOX: Fictional ~2100 scenario content.
3.4 Research Presentation Layer (research_layer)
1. PUBLIC_RESEARCH_SUMMARY: Flagship portfolio entry point (research/keyed-human-machine-hybrid-systems.md & Part XIX) and executive synthesis.
2. THREAT_RESEARCH: Adversarial stress-testing and vulnerability taxonomy (Part XVI, Part XX).
3. DEFENSIVE_DESIGN_REFERENCE: Proposed containment, keying, and refusal protocols (Parts II–XI, XII–XV, XVII–XVIII, XXIII, XXV); not a conformance or deployment finding.
4. CASE_ANALYSIS_RECORD: Ground-0 and institutional case analyses in Parts XII, XVIII, and XXVI; Part XXVI is a controlled counterfactual, and conclusions remain attributed to evidence and method.
5. NARRATIVE_REFERENCE: Fictional-setting material in Part XXIV and locally marked narrative modules in Part XXVII.
6. DERIVATIVE_REFERENCE: Auxiliary summaries and calculations; local metadata identifies provenance and does not upgrade the parent part’s DRAFT status.
4. Summary of Canonical Conceptual Resolutions (specs/normative/canonical-model.md)
1. Canonical Six-Stage Model & Decision Gate (INV-STAGE-001):
   Identity → Representation → Authorization → Continuity → Accountability → Decision (Permit | Refuse)
(Legacy shorthand: Identity → Representation → Authorization → Continuity → Accountability → Refusal, where Refusal names the Stage 6 Decision gate by its default fail-closed branch.)
2. Disambiguated Symbol Namespace & Canonical Permission Score (INV-SYM-001, INV-LEGIT-EQ-001): A(t) denotes Addressability exclusively; Accountability uses K(t)=K_tech(t)×K_ops(t), separate from Legal Responsibility K_legal and Institutional Solvency U_solv. The expanded model is L(t,a)=H(t)×C(t)×K(t)×f(A(t),R(t),S(t,a)), with f=A×R×S. C and K are binary hard gates; the reduced form H×f applies only when C=K=1. L is a proposed normalized permission score, not a measurement of empirical or legal legitimacy. The historical shorthand L(S,t)=A·R·V(S,t) is non-operative.
3. Non-Agency of Computational Components (INV-AGENCY-001): Computational systems never possess or acquire moral or legal agency regardless of processing capability. All legal and moral responsibility remains strictly bound to the keyed human principal (H = 1).
4. Delegation vs. Migration (INV-LEGIT-001): Operational structure and bounded tasks may be inherited or delegated; authority does not migrate. A successor must independently satisfy identity, fresh Human-Key intent, continuity, accountability, and scoped-authorization criteria.
5. OCM Disc → Sphere Equivalence (D² ↪ B³), Resolution Axis (INV-AXIS-001), and Routing Precedence (INV-OCM-PRECEDENCE-001): The 2D Disc (r, θ) is the pedagogical equatorial cross-section; the 3D Sphere (r, θ, φ) is the full operational manifold. Resolution is an authority-resolution mechanism, not an authority source (INV-AXIS-001), with Cost_resolution < Cost_lateral under the Direct Attachment Axiom and Resolution ≻ Coordination as a strict precedence invariant.
6. Discrete Address Ring ℤ_360 (0–359) vs. 360° Closure Notation: Sector addresses occupy 0–359 (0 = Center Origin 0•000•000•0000; 1–359 = peripheral sectors). 360° is never an address slot; it denotes full-cycle topological return to origin (360° ≡ 0° mod 360).
7. Emergency Legitimacy (INV-EMERG-001) & Ground-0 Phase Types (INV-G0-CLASS-001): Emergency conditions do not create authority. NAB, CWO, and GSRB are governance/software labels; AMBIGUOUS and INCOHERENT are diagnostics, not physical or quantum phases. Part XII’s scores are author-applied classifications, not independent findings; Part XXVI contains an explicitly counterfactual B-Side exercise, not an empirical or independent audit.
8. Reclassification of Harshal's English ([TYPE: AUTHORIAL_REGISTER]): Harshal's English is the author's normative prose register and left-to-right reading discipline, distinct from cryptographic/mathematical security primitives ([TYPE: SECURITY_PRIMITIVE], such as the Symbolic Firewall and AGS-IR).
9. Assistive Continuity vs. Prohibited Post-Authorization Actuation (INV-CORPSE-001): A fresh Human-Key protocol response and action-specific intent permit only the scoped operation. H=0 means no current protocol authorization; it does not establish unconsciousness, coercion, or death. Missing or conflicting telemetry fails closed, while identity/provenance is retained and scoped grants may be retired.
10. Two-Layer Medical Governance Boundary & ZKSK Shielded Keying (HS-ZKSK-v1.0): Separates statutory clinical governance from the proposed HMKH protocol. The protocol verifies credentials, freshness, and explicit action-specific intent; it does not diagnose life, consciousness, consent, or coercion. ZK proofs can protect selected data but cannot prove those human states.

Universal Timekeeping System (UTS) — corrected reference module
document_id: HOS-UTS-REF-20261002
provenance_class: DERIVATIVE_BUILD
status_taxonomy: DERIVATIVE_REFERENCE_MODULE
evidence_status: CALCULATED_FROM_STATED_DEFINITIONS
research_layer: DERIVATIVE_REFERENCE
source: Part XX — Supply Chain and Implanted-Device Threat Research; corrected implementation notes dated 2026-10-02.
Purpose and boundary
This module makes the Universal Timekeeping System's duration arithmetic and browser representation internally consistent. It is a derivative reference module, not a new normative time authority. The in-world UTS convention remains FICTION (NARRATIVE_SANDBOX). This module and the UI are DERIVATIVE_BUILD artifacts.
UTS is display-only in HarshalOS. It does not control or attest Ground-0, provenance, Human Key identity/presence/consent, freshness, PDH, authorization, refusal, the Permanent Ledger of Vows, external side effects, or trusted system time. Browser UTC/local time are derived from the device clock. The approximate cosmological epoch below is a model parameter, not an observed exact timestamp.
Duration units
Let c = 299,792,458 m/s, the exact SI speed of light in vacuum. One Universal Second is the time light takes to travel one metre in vacuum:

A UY is not an Earth year. One Julian Earth year of 31,557,600 Earth seconds equals 299,792,458 UY. The 365.25-day convention defines the unit hierarchy; it does not compensate for cosmic expansion.
For s Earth seconds and u Universal Seconds:
u = s × c
s = u / c
UM = u / 60
UH = u / 3,600
UDay = u / 86,400
UY = u / 31,557,600
Examples: 100 UY ≈ 10.52648229 Earth seconds; 150,000,000 US ≈ 4.753213172 UY ≈ 0.500346143 Earth seconds.
Absolute date versus duration
UDay is a duration unit. UDate is an absolute coordinate expressed in UY since a named epoch. Avoid UD as shorthand for both.
The HarshalOS demonstration uses this approximate anchor:
Earth reference instant t₀ = 2026-10-02T00:00:00Z
Approximate age at t₀ = 13,799,000,000 Earth Julian years
UDate(t) = c × [13,799,000,000 + (UTC(t) − t₀) / 31,557,600] UY
UDate(t₀) = 4,136,836,127,942,000,000 UY ≈ 4.136836 × 10^18 UY
The epoch is deliberately approximate. A local Gregorian date/time and Earth UTC are displayed separately from UDate. This is not a cosmological measurement or an external time service.

updates/2026-10-02/02-Frameworks/Universal-Timekeeping-System/UTS-Conversion-Guide.md — worked examples.
updates/2026-10-02/02-Frameworks/Universal-Timekeeping-System/uts_generator.py — Python UTC-to-UTS projection and duration helpers.

index.html, css/uts.css, and js/wm.js — Home Screen local clock, Earth-UTC line, Gregorian month calendar, modeled UDate, and app link.
The browser calculator uses finite JavaScript Number inputs and rounded display. Use arbitrary-precision arithmetic for scientific-grade precision. Original RTF source files are preserved; where their earlier Earth-scale arithmetic or UD overloading conflicts with this corrected reference, use the Markdown specification.

The Grand Architecture — Convergence-era infrastructure architecture module
document_id: GRAND-ARCHITECTURE-REF-20261002
provenance_class: FICTION

source: updates/2026-10-02/ (UpdateOct2) — Grand River Flow Model, Universal Timekeeping System, Convergence Institutions, and the Storm-0558 public-source review; reconciled by CONTINUITY-AUDIT.md and CANONICAL-NUMBERS.md.
1. What The Grand Architecture is
The Grand Architecture (GA) is the single named architecture that binds the four lineages
delivered in the 2026-10-02 update into one structure, and binds that structure back to HarshalOS's
accountability invariants. The update arrived as four unrelated families of material — a
megastructure flow model, a timekeeping system, three institutions, and a threat-intelligence
review — with no architecture stating how they compose. The Grand Architecture is that missing
composition rule.
GA is an architecture of addressability and provenance, not of concrete. It does not design a
dam, a city, an aqueduct, a reactor, or an agency. It states: what layers the setting has, what
address each layer occupies, which numbers are canonical, what invariants keep those numbers
honest, and what the whole structure is not allowed to become inside HarshalOS.
Boundary. GA is FICTION (NARRATIVE_SANDBOX) with DERIVATIVE_BUILD arithmetic anchors. It
is not an engineering design, feasibility finding, water-rights analysis, environmental review,
permit, construction schedule, procurement plan, or claim that any described work exists, is
authorized, or can be built. No GA statement is normative: nothing here enters
specs/normative/, and GA confers no authority,
identity, or production capability on anything.
2. Why a new architecture, and where it sits
Book I already contains the two load-bearing architectures: AGS (Part IV, accountability-gated
systems) and OCM (Part V–VII, radiative addressing and the ℤ₃₆₀ ring). Those are
CANONICAL_SOURCE / NORMATIVE_SPEC. GA is deliberately subordinate to them: it is a
Convergence-era application surface, not a peer or a replacement.

3. The six layers

GA-0 through GA-3 are the setting's physical and civic body. GA-4 and GA-5 are its instrumentation:
one tells it what time it is, the other tells it what it is allowed to believe.
4. Address discipline
The registry is the setting's strongest continuity asset and GA keeps it intact:
Form: 0•100•000•NNNN — orb 100, sector 000, instance NNNN.
Extent: 358 distinct instance values are named in
business plan/Grand Canyon Hydropower Render Spec.md,
partitioned in the update's node mapping as roughly 180 / 120 / 60 across Tiers 1–3.
0•100•000•0000 is held by The Grand River Tribes, not by a machine; 0•100•000•0268 is
Section 7 submerged command; 0•100•000•0176 is the Canyon de Chelly saltwater bio-reserve.
Precision note (GA-INV-002). The instance counter runs 0000–0359 and borrows the
360-count motif, but it occupies the instance field. The canonical ℤ₃₆₀ ring constrains the
sector field DDD ∈ [000, 359] (Part VII, INV-Z360-001). The update's documents sometimes
call the registry "the 360-node ring"; GA records the registry as a 358-entry instance namespace
inside sector 000 and keeps 360° ≡ 0° mod 360 as return-to-origin closure notation, never a
361st slot.

6. Architecture invariants
These are GA's own invariants. They constrain the fiction; they do not modify Book I.
1. GA-INV-001 — Scale is not sovereignty. Population, installed capacity, reservoir volume,
or structural height confer no legitimacy. A GA layer is an addressable object, never an
authority source: H(t) still originates only at Center Origin (0•000•000•0000), and
authority does not migrate; a successor must independently satisfy the current gates (INV-LEGIT-001).
2. GA-INV-002 — Address discipline. Every GA component carries an OCM address in the
documented form; the instance namespace is not the ℤ₃₆₀ sector ring; naming a component creates
no authority for it.
3. GA-INV-003 — Conservation before narrative. Head, flow, and energy are counted once.
Serial tiers do not multiply head; a closed loop is a net consumer, not a generator; the same
water may not be counted at two stages. Where a narrative figure and a mass balance disagree,
the mass balance wins and the narrative figure is labelled superseded.
4. GA-INV-004 — Provenance precedence. Every GA claim carries a provenance class. No GA
statement is promoted to specs/normative/, to the kernel, or to a production control.
5. GA-INV-005 — Evidence discipline. Incident-derived material keeps its claim status
(CONFIRMED, ATTRIBUTED_HYPOTHESIS, UNKNOWN) and its source. A later-challenged hypothesis
is never restated as a confirmed root cause.
6. GA-INV-006 — No deployment, no consent implied. GA asserts no permit, water right,
feasibility finding, construction authorization, or consultation. Named real places, agencies,
universities, and companies are setting references; none has been consulted, and none is
represented as participating.
7. GA-INV-007 — Book II precedence for continuity. The architecture is the library; the novel
is the work in active production. GA is amended to follow the novel, never the reverse.
7. Temporal layer binding (GA-4)
GA uses the corrected UTS reference: UDay is a duration (86,400 US ≈ 288.199378251 μs) and
UDate is an absolute coordinate expressed in UY since an explicitly approximate epoch. The
overloaded UD shorthand is retired. UTS is display-only in HarshalOS: it never controls or
attests Ground-0, provenance, Human Key state, freshness, PDH, authorization, refusal, the
Permanent Ledger of Vows, or trusted system time. See
modules/uts.md.
8. Assurance layer binding (GA-5)
The Storm-0558 package contributes method, not incident findings. Its public-source baseline is
Microsoft's 2023-07-11 disclosure, Microsoft's 2023-09-06 technical account (a **leading
hypothesis**), and the CISA CSRB's 2024-03-20 review (which found no evidence that the impacted key
was in or exfiltrated from a crash dump). GA therefore requires a versioned claim ledger — source,
date, exact claim, evidence status, later qualification, reviewer — and keeps unrelated material
(the September 2024 pager supply-chain attack; Salt Typhoon) attributed and separate. The
conceptual crosswalk to catalogue entries #003 (SCAV++ Output Verification Engine) and #008
(Stingray Counter Protocol) is a review lens; #008 is not a Storm-0558 finding.
9. Institutional layer (GA-3)
GELPA, Celestial Engineers, and Quantum Librarians are fictional bodies in the Convergence
setting. Their oversight relationships, fleets, manufacturing methods, and storage technologies are
story propositions. See modules/convergence-institutions.md. GA
adds one rule: an institution in this layer may be addressed and audited, and may never be cited
as the source of a real obligation, consent, or authorization.

Galactic Environmental and Life Protection Agency (GELPA)
GELPA is a fictional environmental and life-protection body in the human sphere of The Convergence. In the setting, it enforces the fictional Galactic Life Preservation Act, monitors ecosystems, investigates alleged environmental-law breaches, educates the public, and coordinates restoration. Celestial Engineers
Celestial Engineers is a fictional interstellar industry and engineering company. The source material presents it as a shipbuilding and high-technology manufacturer, with automated production, human design teams, and in-world simulation/computing capabilities. These details are narrative worldbuilding, not evidence of actual materials, manufacturing methods, or technical feasibility.
Quantum Librarians
The Quantum Librarians are fictional knowledge stewards. The source describes decentralized “Quantum Libraries,” access as a universal right, curation and preservation, and threats from decay or manipulation. Quantum-state storage and “microConvergence interfaces” are speculative story language, not a description of deployed data-storage technology.
